## Introduction

So far, you've been connecting to OSC through the OnDemand web portal.
However, there is another more basic and universal method to connect to
remote computers: SSH, which is short for Secure Shell.
An [optional self-study page on SSH](../bonus/ssh.qmd) shows you how to directly
use the `ssh` command in a terminal on your own computer to "move" to OSC within
that terminal.

This page, on the other hand, shows you how to connect a
VS Code installation on your computer to OSC using a process called "SSH tunneling".
This connects VS Code to OSC in such a way that not just the terminal but
the entire program operates on OSC.
**Being able to use your own VS Code installation at OSC**
has several advantages over using VS Code Server through OnDemand, such as:

1. You won't have to fill out an OnDemand form every time
2. You can easily have multiple VS Code windows open at the same time
3. You can use the latest version of VS Code "proper" rather than the Server version,
   which has slightly reduced functionality^[Especially the older versions that are installed at OSC.]
4. The same setup also works for [Positron](https://positron.posit.co),
   an R (and Python) IDE that is built on VS Code

We will set up two connections:
one to a **compute node**, which is the one you should normally use,
and one to a **login node**, as a fallback.
Connecting to a compute node takes more setup, but avoids running VS Code
(and anything you do in its terminal) on a login node.

This page is entirely optional:
everything in this course can be done with VS Code Server through OnDemand.

## Install VS Code and the Remote Development extension

1. **Install VS Code** on your own computer:

   - "Regular" installation instructions for
     [Windows](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/setup/windows) /
     [Mac](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/setup/mac) /
     [Linux](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/setup/linux)

   - If you are using an OSU computer, you may not have the required
     "administrative privileges" to install software on your computer the regular way.
     However, you should in that case have an OSU application on your computer that
     allows you to install a selection of approved software,
     and that selection should include VS Code.
     On Windows, this app seems to be simply called "Software Center",
     whereas on Mac, it is called "Ohio State Application Self Service"
     (names likely vary).

2. Open VS Code and install the
   "[**Remote Development extension pack**](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-vscode-remote.vscode-remote-extensionpack)":
   open the Extensions side bar and search for it there.
   Once you found it, click on its `Install` button like you've done previously
   with other extensions.

3. Open a terminal in VS Code (`Terminal` > `New Terminal`):
   you'll need it in the steps below.

## Set up the OSC connections

### The SSH configuration file

1. Open the VS Code **Command Palette**
   (<kbd>F1</kbd> or <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>P</kbd>)
   and start typing "_remote open_":

   - Select "**Remote-SSH: Open SSH Configuration File...**"
   - Then, select the top option, a file that contains the username you have on
     your computer and ends in `.ssh/config`

2. Paste the following into the SSH configuration file that opens:

   ::: {.panel-tabset}
   ### Mac

   ```markdown
   Host osc-pitzer-login
       User <osc-username>
       HostName pitzer.osc.edu

   Host osc-pitzer-compute
       User <osc-username>
       ForwardAgent yes
       StrictHostKeyChecking no
       UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null
       ConnectTimeout 120
       ProxyCommand ssh -o LogLevel=QUIET -o BatchMode=yes osc-pitzer-login ./osc-compute-proxy.sh
   ```

   ### Windows

   ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
   These instructions are for Windows, click "Mac" above to see the Mac instructions.
   (The only difference is the path to the `ssh` program in the last line.)
   :::

   ```markdown
   Host osc-pitzer-login
       User <osc-username>
       HostName pitzer.osc.edu

   Host osc-pitzer-compute
       User <osc-username>
       ForwardAgent yes
       StrictHostKeyChecking no
       UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null
       ConnectTimeout 120
       ProxyCommand C:/Windows/System32/OpenSSH/ssh.exe -o LogLevel=QUIET -o BatchMode=yes osc-pitzer-login ./osc-compute-proxy.sh
   ```
   :::

3. In both instances, change `<osc-username>` to your **OSC username**,
   e.g. to `User jane`. Then, save the file.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### What does this configuration do? _(Click to expand)_

It defines two remote "hosts" at OSC that you can connect to:

- `osc-pitzer-login` connects to a **login node** of OSC's Pitzer cluster.

- `osc-pitzer-compute` connects to a **compute node** of OSC's Pitzer cluster.
  You can't connect directly to a compute node, so this connection first goes to
  a login node, and there runs a script (`osc-compute-proxy.sh`, see below)
  that requests a compute job and then passes on the connection to the compute node
  you've been assigned.
:::

### Avoid being prompted for your OSC password

Next, you'll set up an "SSH key pair",
which lets OSC recognize your computer so you won't be prompted for your password.
This is **required** for the compute node connection,
and convenient for the login node connection and any other SSH connection to OSC.

1. In the VS Code terminal (_regardless of whether you're using Windows or Mac_),
   generate an SSH key pair:

    ``` {.bash}
    ssh-keygen -t rsa
    ```

    You'll get some output and will then be asked several questions,
    but in each case, you can just press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to select the default answer.

2. Transfer the public key to OSC, **replacing `<user>` with your OSC username**.
   You'll be prompted for your OSC password.

   ::: {.panel-tabset}
   ### Mac
   ```bash
   # Replace <user> by your username, e.g. "ssh-copy-id jelmer@pitzer.osc.edu"
   ssh-copy-id <user>@pitzer.osc.edu
   ```

   ### Windows

   ```bash
   # Replace <user> by your username, e.g. "jelmer@pitzer.osc.edu"
   cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub | ssh <user>@pitzer.osc.edu 'mkdir -p .ssh && cat >> .ssh/authorized_keys'
   ```
   :::

3. Test it: the following should print the name of a Pitzer login node,
   _without_ asking for your password:

   ```bash
   ssh osc-pitzer-login hostname
   ```

### The proxy script at OSC

The compute node connection runs a short "proxy script" in your Home dir at OSC.
Copy it there by running the following command in your VS Code terminal:

```bash
ssh osc-pitzer-login 'cp /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/osc-compute-proxy.sh ~/ && chmod +x ~/osc-compute-proxy.sh'
```

This script contains the following:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
exec salloc --quiet -A PAS3493 -t 300 bash -c 'nc $SLURM_NODELIST 22'
```

That is, it requests a compute job (`salloc`) for 300 minutes (5 hours)
with the course's OSC Project `PAS3493`,
and then connects to the compute node you were assigned (`nc ... 22`).

::: {.callout-warning}
#### After the course: change the OSC Project
Once the course is over, you should no longer use the course's OSC Project.
To change the Project, or the duration of your compute jobs,
open `~/osc-compute-proxy.sh` at OSC and edit `PAS3493` and/or `300`.
:::

### Increase the connection timeout

Because it can take a little while to get a compute job,
you also need to increase the time VS Code will wait for a connection:
open the VS Code **Settings** (cog wheel {{< fa cog >}} > `Settings`),
search for `remote.SSH.connectTimeout`, and change its value from 15 to **300** (seconds).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Alternative: the proxy script on your own computer _(Click to expand)_

In our July 2026 workshop, we used a proxy script on participants' own computers
rather than at OSC.
That setup was tested with VS Code and Positron on Mac and Windows,
so use it if the above setup doesn't work for you.
In that case, skip the "proxy script at OSC" step above, and:

1. In the SSH configuration file, change the `ProxyCommand` line for `osc-pitzer-compute` to:

   ::: {.panel-tabset}
   ### Mac

   ```markdown
       ProxyCommand /Users/<computer-username>/.ssh/osc-compute-proxy.sh %h
   ```

   ### Windows

   ```markdown
       ProxyCommand C:/Users/<computer-username>/.ssh/osc-compute-proxy.cmd %h
   ```
   :::

   where `<computer-username>` is your username on your computer
   (it's also in the path to the SSH configuration file).

2. Create the proxy script by running the following in the VS Code terminal:

   ::: {.panel-tabset}
   ### Mac

   ```bash
   cat > ~/.ssh/osc-compute-proxy.sh << 'EOF'
   #!/bin/bash
   exec ssh -o LogLevel=QUIET -o BatchMode=yes osc-pitzer-login \
     "/usr/bin/salloc -A PAS3493 -t 300 /bin/bash -c 'nc \$SLURM_NODELIST 22'" 2>/dev/null
   EOF

   chmod +x ~/.ssh/osc-compute-proxy.sh
   ```

   ### Windows

   ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
   This assumes you are using PowerShell, the default Windows shell in VS Code
   (you should see "PowerShell" in the top right of the terminal).
   If you are using Git Bash or WSL, use the Mac instructions instead.
   :::

   ```powershell
   @'
   @echo off
   ssh -o LogLevel=QUIET -o BatchMode=yes osc-pitzer-login "/usr/bin/salloc -A PAS3493 -t 300 /bin/bash -lc 'nc $SLURM_NODELIST 22'"
   '@ | Out-File -Encoding ascii "$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\osc-compute-proxy.cmd"
   ```
   :::
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Connecting to other OSC clusters
To also connect to Cardinal or Ascend, add additional entries to the SSH configuration file
in which you replace `pitzer` by `cardinal` or `ascend`.
(For the compute node connection, the `ProxyCommand` line should then refer to the
matching login host, e.g. `osc-cardinal-login`.)
:::

## Connect to OSC

### Connecting

1. Open the Command Palette
   (<kbd>F1</kbd> or <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>P</kbd>),
   start typing "_SSH connect_", and click on `Remote-SSH: Connect to Host...`

2. Select **`osc-pitzer-compute`**.

3. A new VS Code window will open.
   The connection may take a little while (typically 5--30 seconds, but longer when
   OSC is busy), because a compute job has to be requested and started.

   - If you're asked about the operating system of the host, select **Linux**.
   - If you're asked whether you "Trust the Authors" of the folder, click "Yes".
   - If there is a pop-up in the bottom-right asking you to update Git,
     click "No" and check "Don't show again".

4. Like you've seen with VS Code Server, the program's default location is your Home dir,
   and it is best to change this using `File` > `Open Folder`:
   go to your `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER` dir.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
If the compute node connection fails or takes more than a few minutes,
use the `osc-pitzer-login` connection instead --- but see the warning below.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
#### When connected to `osc-pitzer-login`, you are on a login node!
With the login node connection, VS Code runs on a login node rather than on a compute node,
so avoid running analyses directly in the terminal, and so on.
:::

### Connecting from now on to previously opened folders

Conveniently, VS Code will remember folders that you've opened this way,
and show them on the "Welcome" tab that is always displayed when you open the program.
Test this:

1. Completely quit VS Code
2. Open it again, and under "Recent" on the Welcome tab,
   look for your folder in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/`,
   and click on that to connect to OSC and open that folder!
